📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
BiasError from oversimplified assumptions; underfitting.
VarianceError from sensitivity to training noise; overfitting.
GeneralizationA model's ability to perform on unseen data.
HyperparameterSetting chosen before training (e.g., tree depth) — distinct from learned parameters.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — the bias-variance checkpoint before advanced ML

WORKED EXAMPLE — diagnose three models at a glance
Same dataset, three fits:
• Model A: train error 22%, val error 23% → both high → high bias (underfit): model too simple → add capacity/features.
• Model B: train 1%, val 19% → big gap → high variance (overfit): regularize, more data, simpler model.
• Model C: train 5%, val 7% → healthy → ship the pipeline forward.
Advanced ML is largely industrialized responses to this table: ensembles and regularization attack variance; deeper architectures and better features attack bias. If you can read train/val curves, every later chapter has a place to hang.
⚠️ THE GAP IS THE DIAGNOSIS
Both-high → bias. Gap → variance. This two-line rule is assumed everywhere in D683 — questions quote error pairs and expect the word.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Advanced ML doesn't start with new algorithms — it starts with knowing exactly where simple ones break. If you can't articulate why a linear model fails on certain problems, you can't motivate the leap to ensembles, deep learning, or transformers.

Core concepts

1. Supervised vs unsupervised. Supervised learning maps inputs to known labels (regression, classification). Unsupervised finds structure without labels (clustering, dim reduction). Most production ML is supervised — you generally have or can collect labels.

2. The bias-variance tradeoff. Bias is error from oversimplified assumptions; variance is sensitivity to training noise. High bias underfits, high variance overfits. Every model decision pushes one up and the other down.

3. Where classical ML fails. Linear models fail on non-linear relationships. Trees overfit. KNN dies in high dimensions. Naive Bayes assumes independence that rarely holds. Each failure motivates an advanced technique.

4. Why ensembles bridge gaps. Combining many imperfect models smooths individual errors. Bagging cuts variance (Random Forest). Boosting cuts both bias and variance (XGBoost). The whole reliably beats any part.

5. When advanced ML helps. Advanced techniques shine on high-dimensional data, non-linear interactions, image/text/audio inputs, and low-signal regimes. Not every problem needs them — start simple.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Reaching for deep learning when a Random Forest would do — tree ensembles often beat NNs on small/medium tabular data.
  • Ignoring the bias-variance lens — picking 'the most complex' model rather than the right one.
  • Confusing 'no labels' with 'unsupervised problem' — often you can label cheaply and convert to supervised.

Quick recap

Advanced ML extends classical ML by addressing specific failure modes: high variance (ensembles), non-linearity (deep learning), sequence structure (RNNs/Transformers), unstructured input (CNNs, embeddings). The bias-variance tradeoff is your North Star.

Glossary

Bias
Error from oversimplified assumptions; underfitting.
Variance
Error from sensitivity to training noise; overfitting.
Generalization
A model's ability to perform on unseen data.
Hyperparameter
Setting chosen before training (e.g., tree depth) — distinct from learned parameters.

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Bootstrap sampleSampling with replacement from training data.
Out-of-fold predictionPrediction made on a held-out fold during cross-validation.
Early stoppingHalting training when validation metric stops improving.
Weak learnerA model only slightly better than chance; building block for boosting.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — bagging, boosting, stacking mechanically

WORKED EXAMPLE — the same 3 learners, three combinators
• Bagging: 200 trees, each trained on a bootstrap resample (+ random feature subsets = random forest), predictions averaged/voted — parallel, cuts VARIANCE.
• Boosting: learner 2 trains on learner 1’s residuals/mistakes, learner 3 on learner 2’s… (gradient boosting/XGBoost) — sequential, cuts BIAS, usually top score on tabular data.
• Stacking: forest + boosting + logistic each predict; a META-model learns from their outputs which to trust where.
Numbers from a churn run: single tree F1 0.71 → forest 0.79 → XGBoost 0.82 → stack 0.83. Diminishing returns, rising complexity — the honest trade to report.
⚠️ STACKING NEEDS CLEAN FOLDS
The meta-model must train on OUT-OF-FOLD predictions of the base models; training it on their in-sample predictions leaks and inflates. That subtlety is the advanced-course question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Ensembles consistently win Kaggle competitions and production tabular ML. Random Forest and XGBoost beat sophisticated single models because errors made by one are corrected by others. Knowing which ensemble fits which problem separates intermediate from advanced practitioners.

Core concepts

1. Bagging. Train many models on bootstrap samples; average predictions. Random Forest is bagging applied to decision trees plus random feature subsets at each split. Reduces variance.

2. Boosting. Train models sequentially, each focusing on errors of previous ones. Gradient Boosting fits new trees to residuals. AdaBoost weights misclassified examples higher. Reduces both bias and variance.

3. Stacking. Train multiple base models, then a meta-learner on their out-of-fold predictions. Best when base models are diverse (e.g., tree + linear + NN).

4. XGBoost / LightGBM / CatBoost. Three optimized gradient-boosted tree libraries. XGBoost: most established. LightGBM: fastest on big data. CatBoost: best out-of-box for categoricals. All dominate tabular ML.

5. When to choose what. Bagging for variance problems. Boosting for max accuracy. Stacking when you have time and diverse base models. Tree ensembles dominate tabular — try these before deep learning.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Boosting too many trees without early stopping — classic overfit. Always pass eval_set + early_stopping_rounds.
  • Using default hyperparameters and assuming XGBoost is automatically better — without tuning, it often loses to a tuned RF.
  • Stacking with correlated base models — they make the same errors, so the ensemble does not help.

Quick recap

Bagging cuts variance via parallel resampling. Boosting cuts bias and variance sequentially. Stacking learns to combine diverse models. For tabular data, gradient boosting is the default first try.

Glossary

Bootstrap sample
Sampling with replacement from training data.
Out-of-fold prediction
Prediction made on a held-out fold during cross-validation.
Early stopping
Halting training when validation metric stops improving.
Weak learner
A model only slightly better than chance; building block for boosting.

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Weight decayEquivalent to L2 regularization in optimizer settings.
Internal covariate shiftDistribution drift in layer activations during training; addressed by batch norm.
OverfittingModel performs much better on train than val/test.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — the modern regularization toolkit

WORKED EXAMPLE — regularizing a deep net that memorizes
Train acc 99%, val 74%. Stack the tools:
• Dropout 0.3 — random neurons silenced per batch → co-adaptation broken.
• Weight decay (L2/AdamW) — large weights taxed.
• Early stopping — halt at the validation-loss minimum.
• Data augmentation — flips/crops/noise multiply effective data (images); synonym swaps/back-translation (text).
• Batch normalization — stabilizes/regularizes as a side effect.
• Label smoothing — soften 1.0 targets to 0.9 so the net stops being overconfident.
After: train 92%, val 86%. Each tool trades a little bias for a lot of variance — tune ONE at a time.
⚠️ AUGMENT ONLY THE TRAINING SET
Augmenting validation/test data corrupts the measurement. And elastic net = L1 + L2 combined — the “which regularizer both selects features and shrinks?” answer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Regularization controls overfitting without throwing away model capacity. Modern ML lives or dies by good regularization — every state-of-the-art deep network combines dropout, weight decay, and data augmentation.

Core concepts

1. L1, L2, ElasticNet. L1 (Lasso) shrinks coefficients toward zero, can produce sparsity. L2 (Ridge) shrinks all coefficients smoothly. ElasticNet combines both. Add penalty terms to your loss; strength is a hyperparameter.

2. Dropout. During training, randomly zero a fraction (0.2-0.5) of activations each forward pass. Forces the network to not rely on any single neuron. Standard for fully-connected layers.

3. Batch normalization. Normalize activations across the mini-batch, then learn an affine transform. Speeds training, reduces internal covariate shift, mild regularizing effect.

4. Early stopping. Track validation loss; stop when it stops improving for N epochs. Implicit regularization — you stop before the model memorizes training noise.

5. Data augmentation. Random transformations on training data (image flips, crops; text paraphrasing). Expands the training set effectively. For images, often beats architectural changes.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Stacking too many regularizers — at some point you starve the model of capacity. Add one at a time and measure.
  • Forgetting model.eval() at inference — dropout and batch norm behave differently in train vs eval mode.
  • Augmentation that destroys label-relevant info (e.g., flipping medical images where left/right matters).

Quick recap

Regularization techniques work together: weight penalties, structural (dropout, batch norm), training (early stopping), data (augmentation). Combine them to control overfitting while keeping model capacity.

Glossary

Weight decay
Equivalent to L2 regularization in optimizer settings.
Internal covariate shift
Distribution drift in layer activations during training; addressed by batch norm.
Overfitting
Model performs much better on train than val/test.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — SGD to Adam, what each fix fixes

WORKED EXAMPLE — the optimizer upgrade path
• Batch GD: exact gradient on ALL data per step — too slow at scale.
• SGD (mini-batch): noisy gradient on 32-256 samples — cheap steps, noise even helps escape shallow minima.
• + Momentum: accumulate a velocity so zigzagging ravines straighten out.
• Adam: momentum + per-parameter adaptive learning rates — the robust default.
• + LR schedules: warmup then decay (cosine) — big steps early, fine steps late.
Reading curves: loss NaN/exploding → LR too high (or add gradient clipping); loss flat → LR too low or dead ReLUs; val loss rising while train falls → overfitting, stop.
⚠️ ADAM ≈ DEFAULT, NOT ALWAYS BEST
Well-tuned SGD+momentum sometimes generalizes better (vision); Adam(W) dominates transformers. The exam wants the trade-off sentence, not a religion.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Choosing the right optimizer can make a model train in 1 hour vs 10 — or fail to converge entirely. Adam is the default for good reason, but knowing when SGD with momentum wins matters for vision and other domains.

Core concepts

1. SGD and momentum. Stochastic Gradient Descent: update weights using gradient on a mini-batch. Momentum adds a velocity term that accelerates in consistent gradient directions. SGD+momentum is still SOTA for vision.

2. Adam and AdamW. Adam: adaptive learning rate per parameter using running estimates of gradient mean/variance. AdamW: Adam with decoupled weight decay. Default for transformers and most NLP.

3. Learning rate schedules. Decay LR over training: step decay, cosine, warmup-then-decay. Warmup is critical for transformers. Schedulers often matter more than the optimizer choice.

4. Vanishing and exploding gradients. Gradients shrink to zero or blow up over many layers. Mitigations: skip connections (ResNet), normalization layers, gradient clipping, careful initialization (Xavier, He).

5. Choosing optimizer per task. Vision/CNNs: SGD+momentum often wins. Transformers/NLP: AdamW. Tabular DL: Adam usually fine. Always tune learning rate first — it dominates other hyperparameters.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting LR warmup with transformers — training diverges in the first hundred steps.
  • Using Adam default LR (1e-3) for transformers — too high; 1e-4 to 5e-5 typical.
  • Not clipping gradients on RNNs — exploding gradients sink training silently.

Quick recap

Optimizers: SGD+momentum still rules vision; AdamW dominates NLP. Learning rate matters more than optimizer choice. Schedules and warmup are essential for stable training.

Glossary

Learning rate
Step size for parameter updates.
Momentum
Running average of past gradients to accelerate optimization.
Gradient clipping
Capping gradient norm to prevent explosions.

Step decay: a learning-rate schedule that reduces the LR at specified EPOCH BOUNDARIES — e.g., divide by 10 at epochs 30 and 60 — big steps early to explore, small steps late to settle.
