🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 Advanced Machine Learning Foundations

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

ML Refresher: Where Advanced ML Begins

⚠ THE GAP IS THE DIAGNOSIS Both-high → bias. Gap → variance. This two-line rule is assumed everywhere in D683 — questions quote error pairs and expect the word.

Ensemble Methods: Bagging, Boosting, Stacking

⚠ STACKING NEEDS CLEAN FOLDS The meta-model must train on OUT-OF-FOLD predictions of the base models; training it on their in-sample predictions leaks and inflates. That subtlety is the advanced-course question.

Advanced Regularization Techniques

⚠ AUGMENT ONLY THE TRAINING SET Augmenting validation/test data corrupts the measurement. And elastic net = L1 + L2 combined — the which regularizer both selects features and shrinks? answer.

Optimization Algorithms in Practice

⚠ ADAM ≈ DEFAULT, NOT ALWAYS BEST Well-tuned SGD+momentum sometimes generalizes better (vision); Adam(W) dominates transformers. The exam wants the trade-off sentence, not a religion.

"},"D683/cheat/c2":{"body":"

📋 Deep Learning Architectures

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Feedforward Networks and Backpropagation

⚠ VANISHING GRADIENTS EXPLAIN THE ARCHITECTURE ZOO Multiplying many small derivatives → early layers learn nothing. ReLU (derivative 1), residual/skip connections, batch norm, and LSTM gates all exist to fight this —…

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)

⚠ CONVOLUTION = LOCAL + SHARED Two exam words: locality (filters see small windows) and weight sharing (same filter everywhere → translation robustness). Output-size arithmetic ((W−F+2P)/S+1) is the standard…

Recurrent Networks and LSTMs

⚠ SEQUENTIAL = SLOW RNNs process token-by-token — no parallelism across the sequence, which (plus long-range limits) is exactly why transformers displaced them. That why transformers won contrast is the exam question.

Transformers and Attention

⚠ Q·K CHOOSES, V CARRIES Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V: queries match keys to decide WEIGHTS; values carry the content. Parallelism + long-range access = why transformers replaced RNNs — the two-sentence exam…

Advanced Architectures: GANs, Autoencoders, Diffusion

⚠ EACH HAS A SIGNATURE FAILURE GAN → mode collapse/instability; autoencoder → blurry reconstructions; diffusion → slow sampling (many denoise steps). Symptom→architecture matching is the exam form.

"},"D683/cheat/c3":{"body":"

📋 Natural Language Processing

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Text Preprocessing and Tokenization

⚠ SUBWORD KILLS OOV Why do modern models use BPE/WordPiece? → no out-of-vocabulary failures + manageable vocab size + shared morphology. The three-part answer the exam wants.

Word and Sentence Embeddings

Core concepts — 1. Word embeddings. Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText: each word gets one vector. Captures static semantic similarity (king - man + woman ≈ queen). Pre-2018 baseline.

Quick recap — Embeddings turn text into vectors capturing semantic meaning. Static (Word2Vec) → contextual (BERT) → sentence-level. Pick a model trained for your task and language.

Glossary

Language Models and Pretraining

⚠ MASKED vs CAUSAL BERT-style = masked LM, bidirectional, best for UNDERSTANDING tasks. GPT-style = causal next-token, unidirectional, best for GENERATION. Matching objective→architecture→use is the exam s repeated…

NLP Tasks: Classification, NER, QA

⚠ TASK TYPE = OUTPUT SHAPE One label → classification. Label per token → NER/tagging. Text span → extractive QA. Generated text → summarization/translation. Identify the output shape and the task (and metric) follows.

"},"D683/cheat/c4":{"body":"

📋 Computer Vision and Multimodal AI

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Image Classification at Scale

⚠ RESNET S TRICK IS THE EXAM FACT Skip connections let layers learn RESIDUALS (adjustments), keeping gradients alive in very deep nets — the one-sentence answer to why did ResNets enable depth?

Object Detection and Segmentation

⚠ SEMANTIC vs INSTANCE Semantic: all cars share one car mask. Instance: car #1 vs car #2 separated. The distinction (and IoU arithmetic) are the two testable items.

Multimodal Models (CLIP, vision-language models)

⚠ CONTRASTIVE = PULL/PUSH How did CLIP learn without labels? → natural captions as supervision, contrastive pull-matching/push-mismatching. Why zero-shot? → classification becomes nearest-text-embedding. Two answers, one mechanism: caption–image pairs align the two embedding spaces, and classification is just retrieval in that shared space.

"},"D683/cheat/c5":{"body":"

📋 Model Deployment and MLOps

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

From Notebook to Production

⚠ REPRODUCIBILITY IS THE FIRST GATE Can anyone retrain this exact model? If code/data/params aren t versioned together, the answer is no — and that s the first thing MLOps questions probe.

Serving Models: APIs, vLLM, TorchServe

⚠ LLM SERVING ≠ CLASSIFIER SERVING Generation is stateful (KV cache) and token-by-token — hence specialized servers (vLLM) and metrics like time-to-first-token. Applying classifier-serving logic to LLMs is the modern…

Monitoring and Drift Detection

⚠ DATA DRIFT CAN PRECEDE PERFORMANCE DROP Input drift is the smoke alarm — it fires BEFORE labels arrive to prove damage. Monitoring only accuracy (which lags by label delay) misses the early warning; that timing…

A/B Testing and Experimentation

⚠ OFFLINE WIN ≠ ONLINE WIN Better validation F1 doesn t guarantee better business metrics (feedback loops, UX effects) — which is WHY live experiments exist. That justification is the graded answer.

"},"D683/cheat/c6":{"body":"

📋 Exam Coverage: Unsupervised Learning

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Unsupervised Learning: Clustering & Dimensionality Reduction

▸ SUPERVISED vs UNSUPERVISED Supervised learns from labeled examples (X → known y): classification, regression. Unsupervised has no labels — it discovers structure: clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection.

"},"D683/cheat/c7":{"body":"

📋 Ethical AI and Responsible Deployment

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Bias and Fairness in ML

⚠ REMOVING THE SENSITIVE COLUMN ISN T ENOUGH Proxies (ZIP, names, purchase patterns) reconstruct it — fairness through unawareness fails. Auditing OUTCOMES by group is the required practice and the exam answer.

Privacy: Differential Privacy and Federated Learning

⚠ EPSILON IS THE PRIVACY DIAL Smaller ε = stronger privacy = noisier answers/less accuracy. And federated ≠ automatically private — updates leak without DP/secure aggregation. Both caveats are exam material.

Explainability and Transparency

⚠ LOCAL vs GLOBAL Why THIS prediction? → local (SHAP/LIME per instance). What drives the model overall? → global (importances). Matching question-to-scope is the repeated exam item.

AI Safety and Adversarial Robustness

⚠ IMPERCEPTIBLE ≠ HARMLESS Adversarial examples exploit the gap between human and model perception — tiny pixel changes, huge prediction changes. Why do they work? → models rely on brittle, non-robust features. Safety…

Capstone: End-to-End Advanced ML Project

Core concepts — 1. Problem framing. Translate a business need into a precise ML problem: input X, output y, metric, success threshold. Most failed ML projects fail here.

Quick recap — A capstone synthesizes problem framing, data, modeling, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring. Document trade-offs, present honestly, name limits.

Glossary — Where the ROI usually is: improving the DATA first — cleaning, labels, features — typically beats swapping in a fancier model. And a simple baseline is valuable even when it loses — it tells you how much of the problem is easy and whether the complex model earns its cost.
